reviewBoundary: Six new whole readings in three senior practices, three plus four questions each. Original fictional notices/narratives and explicitly illustrative scenarios; general footprint explanations contain no invented studies or numerical findings. Author checks evidence, alternatives and candidate positions. No independent teacher or learner calibration claimed.

units.title: A photo challenge and a study corner
units.alignmentNote: Two whole new readings, three and four questions, follow the National I practice structure. The recorded original supplies level/family drafting context only; no source text, keys or sample-count increase is claimed.

materials.title: A. The same place, twice
materials.text:
The town youth centre invites students aged thirteen to eighteen to enter its photography challenge, The Same Place, Twice. Choose a place you can visit safely and take two photographs at different times. The contrast might come from weather, light, activity or your own position.

Submit both images with a caption of 80-120 words explaining what changed and why you chose the pair. The photographs must be taken by you during this year's challenge period, 1-30 April. Older holiday photographs are not eligible. You may adjust brightness and crop the images, but do not add or remove people or objects digitally.

Entries close at 18:00 on 2 May. Use the centre's online form and upload two JPEG files, each no larger than five megabytes. Do not send printed photographs to the centre. A parent or guardian must approve entries from students under sixteen.

Judges will consider the relationship between the two pictures and the explanation, rather than the cost of the camera used. A phone camera is acceptable. Selected pairs will be displayed in the centre in June; photographers will be contacted before any display is arranged.

You may work with a friend when choosing a location, but each entry must contain one person's own photographs and caption. One entry per student is allowed. If access to the online form is difficult, ask centre staff for help before the closing date.

questions.prompt: What must an entry contain?
options: Four images of different places without a caption
Two self-taken photographs and an explanation of their relationship
One old holiday photograph and a newly edited copy
A printed photograph taken by a friend
questions.explanation: The challenge requires two own photographs of one place plus an80-120-word caption. Old images, another photographer's work and four unrelated images fail the conditions.

questions.prompt: Which digital change is allowed?
options: Combining several people from separate images
Cropping an image
Removing a person from a photograph
Adding an object that was not there
questions.explanation: Cropping and brightness adjustment are allowed. Adding/removing people or objects and combining inserted people cross the stated editing limit.

questions.prompt: How will entries be judged?
options: Mainly by the price of the camera
By how early the student bought a camera
Only by the number of people shown
By the pair's connection and the explanation
questions.explanation: Judges focus on the relationship and caption. Camera price is explicitly not the basis; crowd count and purchase timing are not criteria.

materials.title: B. Asking for a quiet hour
materials.text:
As examinations approached, I began carrying my books from room to room in search of silence. My brother practised the recorder in the bedroom we shared. The television played in the living room, and somebody was always opening the kitchen door. I decided that nobody understood how much I needed to study.

One evening, I closed my book loudly and announced that I would go to the library. Mum looked at the clock. It would close in twenty minutes. She asked which part of the evening was hardest for me. I had expected her to defend the television, not to ask for a useful detail.

I explained that I could manage ordinary conversation, but the recorder made it difficult to concentrate on reading. My brother had assumed that wearing my headphones meant I could not hear him. He offered to practise earlier, before I came home. Mum suggested one quiet hour after dinner, when we could all do something without music or television.

The first evening did not become perfectly silent. A neighbour's dog barked, and someone dropped a pan upstairs. Yet I finished more reading than I had the night before. My family had not changed the whole building. They had changed the part of the evening we could arrange together.

After my examinations, I asked whether my brother needed quiet while learning a difficult piece. He said he mostly needed a patient listener. So I sat with him for a while. I had spent days treating my family as obstacles to my work. A precise request helped us discover something more useful: different needs did not always conflict, once we had actually explained them.

questions.prompt: What had the writer initially assumed about the family?
options: They wanted everyone to move to the library.
They deliberately wanted the writer to fail.
They did not understand the need to study.
They had already planned a quiet hour.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the writer thought nobody understood. Deliberate sabotage is a stronger unsupported claim, and a quiet hour or library plan had not yet been agreed.

questions.prompt: Why had the brother continued practising nearby?
options: He thought the headphones blocked the sound.
He could play only when the television was on.
He believed the examinations had finished.
He was forbidden to practise before dinner.
questions.explanation: He assumed the headphones prevented hearing him. The other restrictions and beliefs are not stated.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the dog and the dropped pan?
options: To show the family's arrangement was useless.
To explain why the library remained necessary.
To show that improvement did not require complete silence.
To identify the main causes of all study problems.
questions.explanation: Uncontrollable sounds remain, yet reading improves. A contradicts the positive result; B exaggerates incidental noise; C ignores the successful home arrangement.

questions.prompt: What does the writer learn?
options: Headphones always remove surrounding noise.
Specific communication can reveal workable ways to meet different needs.
A complaint is most useful when it blames the loudest person.
Everyone needs silence for the same activities.
questions.explanation: Explaining the particular difficulty leads to coordinated changes and later understanding the brother's different need. A imposes sameness, B blame and D a false technical guarantee.

units.title: Field kits and footprints
units.alignmentNote: Two whole new readings, three and four questions, follow the National I practice structure. The recorded original supplies level/family drafting context only; no source text, keys or sample-count increase is claimed.

materials.title: A. Borrow a field-study kit
materials.text:
Riverside Nature Centre lends small field-study kits to visitors who want to observe the local area more closely. A kit contains a magnifying glass, a simple measuring tape, a notebook and a laminated guide to making observations. It does not include binoculars, collecting containers or protective clothing.

Borrowers must be sixteen or above. A younger visitor may use a kit when an adult makes the booking and remains responsible for it. There is no hire charge, but a twenty-pound deposit is required. It is returned when the complete kit is checked back in without damage.

Normal loans last forty-eight hours. Because the centre is closed on Sunday, kits collected after 15:00 on Friday may be returned by 10:00 on Monday. Please arrange the return time with staff when collecting; leaving a kit outside the closed building does not count as returning it.

You may record, sketch and photograph what you find. The kits are designed for observation, not removing plants or animals. Stay on public paths and follow any temporary closure notices. Wet-weather footwear should be your own.

Reserve a kit by telephone at least a day before collection. We cannot guarantee same-day availability. Staff can show you how to use the items and suggest a suitable starting route, but the loan does not include a guided walk. If a kit item is already damaged, report it before leaving the desk.

questions.prompt: How may a fourteen-year-old use a kit?
options: By booking alone and paying a larger deposit
With an adult who books and remains responsible
By leaving identity documents outside the centre
Only after joining a paid guided walk
questions.explanation: A younger user needs an adult booking and responsibility. A larger deposit does not replace that condition; guided walks are not included, and no identity-document procedure is stated.

questions.prompt: When may a kit collected at 16:00 Friday be returned under the special rule?
options: After a full week without arrangement
Only before 16:00 Saturday
By 10:00 Monday
At any time on Sunday outside the building
questions.explanation: Friday-after15:00 loans have the Monday10:00 deadline. Sunday is closed and outside deposits do not count; neither the shortened Saturday rule nor an unrestricted week is stated.

questions.prompt: Which item should a visitor provide personally?
options: Wet-weather footwear
The included measuring tape
The laminated observation guide
The included notebook
questions.explanation: Protective clothing and footwear are not included. The tape, guide and notebook are explicitly part of the kit.

materials.title: B. Reading the ground
materials.text:
A footprint can be an invitation to imagine an animal passing unseen. It can also tempt an observer to say more than the ground really supports. A single mark may suggest a paw, but its depth alone does not reveal the animal's weight. A small animal on soft mud can leave a deeper impression than a heavier one crossing firm ground.

The surface is therefore part of the evidence. Before comparing prints, an observer needs to ask whether they were made under similar conditions. Water, loose sand and a hard layer beneath the surface can all affect the resulting shape. A mark is produced by an interaction between a foot and the material it presses, not by the foot in isolation.

A series of tracks may tell more than one print. Their spacing and pattern can offer clues about movement, and repeated details may help an observer distinguish a consistent feature from an accidental distortion. Even so, a path used by several animals can contain overlapping journeys. What appears to be one trail may require more careful examination.

Absence needs caution too. An animal crossing a rock may leave little visible trace. Later rain or human footsteps can remove marks that were once clear. Finding no tracks is not automatically evidence that no animal has passed. It may instead reveal something about where or when you looked.

For these reasons, a useful field note includes the location, surface and recent conditions as well as a sketch or photograph. Such information lets another person understand what the observer actually encountered. It also makes uncertainty visible: one may be confident about the pattern while remaining unsure of the species.

This care does not remove the pleasure of discovery. It extends it. Instead of turning every mark into an instant answer, the observer gains several better questions to carry along the next stretch of path.

questions.prompt: Why is depth alone insufficient for judging the animal's weight?
options: Every animal creates an identical mark.
Footprints never preserve any physical information.
The ground's condition also affects the impression.
Only the observer's imagination determines depth.
questions.explanation: Soft and firm surfaces produce different depths for different loads. A and B overstate unreliability or sameness; C ignores the physical interaction described.

questions.prompt: What advantage may a series of tracks offer?
options: A guarantee that the species can be named immediately
Patterns that help interpret movement and repeated features
Proof that only one animal used the path
Evidence unaffected by later weather
questions.explanation: Spacing and repeated details provide more clues. Overlapping trails prevent a one-animal guarantee; species may remain uncertain and weather can alter evidence.

questions.prompt: What does a lack of visible tracks establish?
options: Only a limited observation requiring attention to surface and timing
That every earlier observer was mistaken
That animals cannot walk across rock
That no animal has visited the place
questions.explanation: Marks may not form or may disappear. A and B claim too much, and D contradicts the rock example.

questions.prompt: How does the author view careful field notes?
options: As a requirement to identify every species
As a way to support interpretation while preserving uncertainty
As an obstacle to enjoying nature
As a substitute for observing the ground
questions.explanation: Notes give context and identify limits without removing discovery's pleasure. They do not replace observation or force certainty about species.

units.title: A project fund and words in context
units.alignmentNote: Two whole new readings, three and four questions, follow the National I practice structure. The recorded original supplies level/family drafting context only; no source text, keys or sample-count increase is claimed.

materials.title: A. Small projects, shared places
materials.text:
The Eastbank Youth Fund offers grants of up to four hundred pounds for small projects that improve a shared local place. Applications may come from school groups or youth clubs. Projects for one person's private collection or holiday are not eligible.

Each application must name at least three young participants and an adult contact. Explain the place, the people who use it and the specific change you hope to make. Include a simple budget based on actual prices. The fund can cover materials and essential public-transport journeys, but not wages, meals or new personal phones.

Projects must not begin before a decision is received. Spending already made cannot be claimed back. Successful applicants will hear by 1 June and may begin from 1 July. Work must be completed by 30 September. If a delay becomes likely, contact the fund before the completion date rather than assume an extension.

Applications close on 15 May. A short description of how the place will be used matters more than an impressive title. The panel may ask for a brief conversation with group members before making its decision.

Keep receipts for purchases. Within two weeks of completion, send a short account of what was done, what the group learned and how much was spent. Unused money must be returned. Photographs can help explain a project, but are not compulsory. The panel understands that not every useful improvement is visually dramatic.

questions.prompt: Which proposed project is eligible in principle?
options: A school group improving a shared seating area after approval
A group seeking repayment for a completed holiday
A student buying objects for a private collection
A club that started the work before receiving a decision
questions.explanation: A shared-place project by a school group starting after approval meets the central conditions. Private collections, holidays and already-started work are excluded.

questions.prompt: Which expense may the grant cover?
options: A new personal phone for each member
Materials needed for the approved improvement
Wages for the young participants
All meals during the summer holiday
questions.explanation: Materials are eligible. Personal phones, wages and meals are explicitly not covered.

questions.prompt: What must the group do after completing its project?
options: Wait until the next year to report spending
Submit photographs even if they do not explain the work
Keep any unspent funds for an unrelated private project
Send an account and return any unused money
questions.explanation: An account is due within two weeks and unused money returned. Reporting next year is too late, photographs are optional and private diversion is not allowed.

materials.title: B. More than a dictionary entry
materials.text:
Suppose someone says, "That was clever." After a friend solves a difficult puzzle, the words may be straightforward praise. After the friend leaves both train tickets at home, the same words may express irritation. The dictionary meaning has not become useless. It is the contrast between that positive meaning and the situation that makes the second remark work.

For a language learner, the temptation is to seek a separate translation for every possible use. Yet an endless list would still fail to describe every conversation. Understanding often requires noticing who is speaking, what has happened and what response the speaker seems to invite. The phrase is an action within an exchange, not simply a label attached to an event.

In speech, tone can help. On a page, writers may supply other clues: a pause before the reply, an unexpected reaction or a detail that makes the literal reading difficult. None of these clues should be treated as a mechanical code. A pause can indicate hesitation, surprise or a person searching for a word. Several details need to be considered together.

Context does not give readers permission to make a sentence mean anything they choose. Interpretations still need support from the words and the circumstances described. If a reading requires ignoring several details, it is weaker than one that explains them. Recognising irony depends on a shared conventional meaning, not on abandoning meaning altogether.

Sometimes the available fragment simply does not settle the question. Without knowing whether the tickets were actually lost or whether the friends were joking about an imaginary mistake, a reader may reasonably remain uncertain. That uncertainty is different from knowing nothing: the reader can identify which further information would matter.

A good dictionary remains useful, but fluent reading involves another habit too. Instead of stopping once a word has been recognised, ask what its use is doing here. The answer may confirm the first meaning that came to mind, or require a more careful account of how the sentence fits its scene.

questions.prompt: Why does the author use the two examples of That was clever?
options: To argue that praise is always dishonest
To provide two unrelated dictionary definitions of train
To prove the expression has no conventional meaning
To illustrate how a situation changes what familiar words do
questions.explanation: The same positive expression functions differently in puzzle success and forgotten tickets. Conventional meaning remains essential; train definitions and universal dishonesty are not the argument.

questions.prompt: What does the discussion of a pause suggest?
options: It always signals irony.
It is one clue that must be considered with other details.
It is meaningful only when accompanied by a picture.
It should be ignored in written texts.
questions.explanation: A pause has several possible functions and should be combined with context. A imposes a mechanical code, B discards a useful clue and C adds an unstated picture requirement.

questions.prompt: What limits a reasonable interpretation, according to the author?
options: The length of the dictionary entry alone
Support from the words and described circumstances
The reader's ability to imagine any alternative scene
A rule that every positive word must express praise
questions.explanation: Interpretation needs evidence from language and situation. Imagination alone is insufficient, positive words can be ironic and dictionary length does not decide a particular use.

questions.prompt: How should a reader respond when a fragment leaves the meaning uncertain?
options: Assume the writer has made a spelling error
Choose the most dramatic explanation as a fact
Identify what further information would help
Discard every conventional meaning
questions.explanation: The author values locating the missing information rather than pretending certainty. Drama, abandoning meaning and assuming a spelling error are not warranted responses.
